# Iceland Westfjords 2026

## Overview

Ten days in the Westfjords in June 2026, in a small estate car with a roof box and a tent in the back. The far north-west is the quietest part of the country I have seen, a maze of fjords where the road follows the water in and out and a short distance on the map takes an hour to drive. I came for the cliffs and the bird life and left with a list of places I did not reach. The light in June barely leaves, and I ate dinner at ten in the evening under a pale sky more than once.

I took a ferry across one of the wide fjord mouths to save a long loop of driving, and used the tunnels where they exist, because the alternative is a detour of a hundred kilometres or more. The weather changed between the fjords, sun on one side and rain on the next, and I learned to check the forecast for the specific village rather than the region. I paid about 85 EUR a night for the guesthouses I used and spent the rest of the nights in the tent for 20 EUR a pitch. The guesthouses were small and friendly, and the owners gave better advice on the roads than any app. I would bring a warmer sleeping bag for the tent nights next time, because the coast wind is cold even in the middle of summer.

## Route

I began by crossing from the south to Stykkishólmur and taking the Baldur ferry from Stykkishólmur to Brjánslækur, the crossing that saves the long drive around the wide bay. It takes about three hours, and I spent most of it on deck watching the islands slide past and a pair of dolphins working the wake. Booking ahead matters in summer, because the car deck fills and a missed sailing means a day lost.

From the landing I drove north through the fjords to Dynjandi, the waterfall that fans out over a tiered cliff like a bridal veil. The walk up from the car park takes twenty minutes and each level gives a different view; the spray soaked me to the knees. The Vestfjarðagöng tunnel charges a toll of about 12 EUR, paid online afterwards, and there is no booth at the mouth, so I noted the plate and settled it the next evening from the laptop. The tunnel runs for kilometres under the mountain and comes out in a valley I had not expected.

From there I pushed to Ísafjörður, the largest town in the region, where I spent two nights and walked the old trading street. The last long drive took me south-west along the coast to the cliffs at Látrabjarg, the westernmost point, where the seabirds nest in their thousands and the edge drops straight to the sea. I lay on my stomach at the rim and watched puffins come and go for an hour. The road out to the cliffs is gravel and slow, and I turned back before the last stretch when the fog closed in. The drive from Ísafjörður south to the cliffs is the longest single stretch and the one to do in the morning, so the light is behind you and the fog has not yet rolled in. I filled the tank before I left the town, because the pumps after it are few.

## Costs

The ferry from Stykkishólmur to Brjánslækur was about 55 EUR with the car, the single biggest fixed cost of the route and cheap for the ground it saves. The tunnel toll at Vestfjarðagöng came to about 12 EUR, paid online after the fact. Fuel ran near 300 EUR for the ten days, the estate car averaging well enough but the fjord roads eating the difference. Guesthouses were 85 EUR a night and I used four of them; the tent pitches were 20 EUR each and I used five.

Food I mostly cooked at the campsites and in guesthouse kitchens, about 25 EUR a day from the supermarkets, with three meals out at roughly 40 EUR each. Entry to the cliffs and the waterfall was free, as it usually is in Iceland. The total for the ten days came to about 1900 EUR, a little over what I had set aside, and the ferry and the fuel were the two lines I had underestimated. The campsites took a card at the little kiosks, and the showers cost a coin or two. I would set aside an extra 100 EUR for the ferry crossing and the tunnels, which are easy to forget when you budget for fuel alone.
